title: Cannabinoids for medical use: A systematic review and meta-analysis

claims.statement: In randomized trials of people receiving chemotherapy (28 trials, 1,772 participants, mostly of nabilone, THC, levonantradol or dronabinol; 23 at high and 5 at unclear risk of bias), cannabinoid medicines compared with placebo are associated with more people having complete control of nausea and vomiting: in a 2015 meta-analysis of the three placebo-controlled parallel-group trials that could be pooled (dronabinol or nabiximols; Whiting et al., 2015; AMSTAR 2 critically low), 47% on cannabinoids against 20% on placebo had a complete response (the abstract's crude averages, their derivation not described; about 27 more in 100, editors' arithmetic), OR 3.82 (95% CI 1.55 to 9.42; 102 patients; I2 0%; low certainty by the review team). Twenty trials compared cannabinoids only with other anti-sickness medicines, most often prochlorperazine (15 trials), and these comparisons are not pooled in the article, so how cannabinoids compare with the anti-sickness medicines in use is not shown here. A narrative review calls THC an effective treatment for nausea and vomiting with chemotherapy and says patients often find marijuana more effective (Volkow et al., 2014; second-hand). Certainty: low. Status: replicated.
claims.magnitude: Whiting et al. 2015, cannabinoid (dronabinol or nabiximols) against placebo, parallel-group trials, random effects: complete response 47% vs 20% (the abstract's crude averages; about 27 more in 100, editors' arithmetic), OR 3.82 (95% CI 1.55 to 9.42; 3 trials, 102 patients; I2 0%; GRADE low by the review team). Comparisons with active anti-sickness medicines (20 trials) not pooled in the article.

claims.statement: In randomized trials of adults with chronic pain, mostly neuropathic or cancer pain (28 trials, 2,454 participants; 17 at high and 9 at unclear risk of bias), cannabinoid medicines, mostly nabiximols (a THC and CBD spray used in the mouth), compared with placebo in trials with follow-up of at most 15 weeks, are associated with a small reduction in pain. In a 2015 meta-analysis of the parallel-group trials (Whiting et al., 2015; AMSTAR 2 critically low), 37% of people on cannabinoids and 31% on placebo had their pain reduced by at least 30% (the abstract's crude averages, their derivation not described; about 6 more in 100, editors' arithmetic), an odds ratio of 1.41 (95% CI 0.99 to 2.00; 8 trials, 7 of them of nabiximols and 1 of smoked THC, 1,370 people; I2 48%) that does not exclude no difference, and pain on a 0 to 10 scale was 0.46 points lower with nabiximols (95% CI 0.11 to 0.80 lower; 6 trials, 948 people; I2 59%); the review team rated both moderate certainty and set no threshold for a clinically important change. The one smoked-THC trial gave the largest responder effect (OR 3.43, 1.03 to 11.48). More people rated themselves improved overall (OR 2.08, 1.21 to 3.59; 6 trials, 267 people; low certainty by the review team), neuropathic-pain scale scores were 3.89 points lower on a 0 to 100 scale (0.47 to 7.32 lower), and the Brief Pain Inventory (-0.17, -0.50 to 0.16) and quality of life (EQ-5D, -0.01, -0.05 to 0.02) did not differ. The review concludes that moderate-quality evidence supports cannabinoids for chronic pain, but the outcomes so rated are either not statistically significant or small. Certainty: low. Status: replicated.
claims.magnitude: Whiting et al. 2015, parallel-group trials, random effects, cannabinoid against placebo: at least 30% pain reduction 37% vs 31% (the abstract's crude averages; about 6 more in 100, editors' arithmetic), OR 1.41 (95% CI 0.99 to 2.00; 8 trials, 1,370 patients; I2 48%; GRADE moderate by the review team); smoked-THC trial OR 3.43 (1.03 to 11.48); neuropathic pain OR 1.38 (0.93 to 2.03; 6 trials); nabiximols: 0 to 10 pain scale WMD -0.46 (-0.80 to -0.11; 6 trials, 948 patients; I2 59%; moderate); Brief Pain Inventory -0.17 (-0.50 to 0.16; 3 trials); Neuropathic Pain Scale -3.89 on 0 to 100 (-7.32 to -0.47; 5 trials); global impression of change OR 2.08 (1.21 to 3.59; 6 trials, 267 patients; I2 68%; low); EQ-5D -0.01 (-0.05 to 0.02; 3 trials).

claims.statement: In randomized trials of people with multiple sclerosis (11 trials, 2,138 participants; 3 further trials in paraplegia, 142 participants, could not be pooled; of all 14 trials, 7 at high and 5 at unclear risk of bias), cannabinoid medicines, mostly nabiximols, compared with placebo in trials with follow-up of at most 15 weeks, are associated with a small improvement in spasticity as patients rate it, but not detectably as clinicians measure it. In a 2015 meta-analysis (Whiting et al., 2015; AMSTAR 2 critically low), patients' own spasticity ratings on 0 to 10 scales were 0.76 points lower (95% CI 0.14 to 1.38 lower; 3 trials, 698 people; I2 73%; low certainty by the review team) and more patients rated themselves improved overall (OR 1.44, 1.07 to 1.94; 3 trials, 461 people; low), while the Ashworth scale, a clinician's rating of muscle tone, did not clearly change (-0.12, -0.24 to 0.01; 5 trials, 1,244 people; I2 0%; moderate; the corrected value), nor did the share of people whose rated spasticity fell by at least 30% (OR 1.64, 0.95 to 2.83) or 50% (1.40, 0.81 to 2.41; 2 trials each), activities of daily living (Barthel index, -0.58, -1.73 to 0.56; 4 trials) or walking speed (-0.86, -3.08 to 1.36; 2 trials). The review concludes that moderate-quality evidence supports cannabinoids for spasticity, but the outcome rated moderate (Ashworth) showed no clear difference. Certainty: low. Status: replicated.
claims.magnitude: Whiting et al. 2015, multiple sclerosis trials, random effects, against placebo: patient-rated spasticity (0 to 10) WMD -0.76 (95% CI -1.38 to -0.14; 3 trials, 698 patients; I2 73%; GRADE low by the review team); global impression of change OR 1.44 (1.07 to 1.94; 3 trials, 461 patients; low); Ashworth WMD -0.12 (-0.24 to 0.01; 5 trials, 1,244 patients; I2 0%; moderate; corrected value, Table 2 still prints -0.11, -0.23 to 0.02); 30% reduction OR 1.64 (0.95 to 2.83) and 50% reduction OR 1.40 (0.81 to 2.41), 2 trials each (low); Barthel -0.58 (-1.73 to 0.56; 4 trials; moderate); walking speed -0.86 (-3.08 to 1.36; 2 trials; moderate).

claims.statement: For sleep problems, appetite and weight in HIV, anxiety, depression, psychosis, glaucoma and Tourette syndrome, randomized trials of cannabinoid medicines compared with placebo or other treatments are too few, small or short to show whether they help: in a 2015 meta-analysis (Whiting et al., 2015; AMSTAR 2 critically low), each of these conditions had one to four trials designed for it (four for appetite in HIV, at most two for each of the others) and none for depression, most of them small and many at high risk of bias. Sleep: in 19 placebo-controlled trials for chronic pain or multiple sclerosis, mainly of nabiximols, sleep-quality scores differed from placebo by -0.58 points (95% CI -0.87 to -0.29; 8 trials) and sleep-disturbance scores by -0.26 (-0.52 to 0.00; 3 trials), both very low certainty by the review team; of two trials in sleep problems (54 participants), one in sleep apnoea (22 patients; attributed to nabilone in the review, although its reference list points to a dronabinol trial) reported a lower apnoea–hypopnoea index (-19.64, P = .02), and a crossover trial in fibromyalgia found nabilone better than amitriptyline for insomnia (-3.25, -5.26 to -1.24); the review concludes, on low-quality evidence, that cannabinoids may improve sleep. Appetite in HIV: weight gain of 2 kg or more within 6 weeks with dronabinol against placebo, OR 2.2 (0.68 to 7.27; 1 trial, 88 patients), among 4 trials all at high risk of bias. Anxiety: one trial of cannabidiol in 24 people with social anxiety disorder, measured during a simulated public-speaking test with 107 minutes of follow-up (anxiety factor -16.52, P = .01; very low). Depression: in 5 trials for other conditions, 3 found no difference and one found worse depression scores at the highest nabiximols dose (2.50, 0.38 to 4.62) but not at the two lower doses (very low). Psychosis: two trials of cannabidiol (71 participants) found no difference, with intervals too wide to show the absence of an effect (against amisulpride, BPRS -0.10, -9.20 to 8.90; 35 patients). Glaucoma: one crossover trial of 6 people found no difference in eye pressure. Tourette syndrome: two small trials of THC capsules (36 participants) suggested less tic severity on some scales (17 or 18 patients per analysis; low). Epilepsy was not among the review's conditions; a narrative review describes only a parent survey of cannabidiol-rich cannabis in childhood epilepsy, in which 2 of 19 families reported freedom from seizures, and says safety and efficacy data were insufficient (Volkow et al., 2014; second-hand). Certainty: very low. Status: mixed.
claims.magnitude: Whiting et al. 2015 (GRADE ratings by the review team): sleep quality WMD -0.58 (95% CI -0.87 to -0.29; 8 trials; very low) and sleep disturbance -0.26 (-0.52 to 0.00; 3 trials; very low) in trials for other conditions; sleep apnoea, apnoea–hypopnoea index -19.64 (P = .02; 22 patients; low); fibromyalgia insomnia, nabilone against amitriptyline -3.25 (-5.26 to -1.24), restfulness 0.48 (0.01 to 0.95); HIV weight gain of 2 kg or more, OR 2.2 (0.68 to 7.27; 1 trial, 88 patients; low); social anxiety, anxiety factor -16.52 (P = .01; 24 patients; very low); depression, highest nabiximols dose 2.50 (0.38 to 4.62), single-trial HADS 0.15, MADRS 1.90 and BDI 0.69 (all non-significant; very low); psychosis, cannabidiol against amisulpride BPRS -0.10 (-9.20 to 8.90) and PANSS 1 (-12.60 to 14.60; 35 patients; low); glaucoma, 1 crossover trial of 6, no difference; Tourette syndrome, single-trial differences on four tic scales with 17 or 18 patients (P = .03, P < .05, P = .061, P = .008; low).

claims.statement: In randomized trials of cannabinoid medicines for many conditions (62 trials reported adverse events), cannabinoids at the highest dose each trial tested, compared with placebo or another medicine, increase short-term side effects: in a 2015 meta-analysis (Whiting et al., 2015; AMSTAR 2 critically low), the odds of any adverse event were 3.03 times higher (95% CI 2.42 to 3.80; 29 studies, 3,714 patients; I2 31%), of a serious adverse event 1.41 times (1.04 to 1.92; 34 studies, 3,248 patients; I2 0%) and of leaving a trial because of adverse events 2.94 times (2.18 to 3.96; 23 studies, 2,755 patients), with no difference in deaths (1.01, 0.51 to 2.00; 5 studies, 929 patients). Specific effects more frequent with cannabinoids included disorientation (OR 5.41, 2.61 to 11.19), dizziness (5.09, 4.10 to 6.32; 41 studies), euphoria (4.08, 2.18 to 7.64), confusion (4.03, 2.05 to 7.97), drowsiness (3.68, 2.24 to 6.01), dry mouth (3.50, 2.58 to 4.75), somnolence (2.83, 2.05 to 3.91), loss of balance (2.62, 1.12 to 6.13), hallucination (2.19, 1.02 to 4.68; 10 studies), nausea (2.08, 1.63 to 2.65), asthenia (2.03, 1.35 to 3.06), fatigue (2.00, 1.54 to 2.62), vomiting (1.67, 1.13 to 2.47) and diarrhoea (1.65, 1.04 to 2.62); depression, anxiety, paranoia, psychosis and seizures did not differ clearly, with wide intervals (psychosis 1.09, 0.07 to 16.35; 2 studies, 37 patients). The review reports odds ratios only, not how many people in 100 had each effect; using the highest dose was the authors' choice of a worst case; and no study of long-term adverse events was found, even among non-randomized studies. Certainty: moderate. Status: replicated.
claims.magnitude: Whiting et al. 2015, cannabinoid (highest dose) against placebo or active comparator, all indications: any adverse event OR 3.03 (95% CI 2.42 to 3.80; 29 studies, 3,714 patients; I2 31%); serious 1.41 (1.04 to 1.92; 34 studies, 3,248 patients; I2 0%); withdrawal due to adverse events 2.94 (2.18 to 3.96; 23 studies, 2,755 patients); death 1.01 (0.51 to 2.00; 5 studies, 929 patients); psychiatric disorders 3.10 (1.81 to 5.29; 8 studies); nervous system disorders 3.17 (2.20 to 4.58; 10 studies). Individual events: disorientation 5.41 (2.61 to 11.19); dizziness 5.09 (4.10 to 6.32); euphoria 4.08 (2.18 to 7.64); confusion 4.03 (2.05 to 7.97); drowsiness 3.68 (2.24 to 6.01); dry mouth 3.50 (2.58 to 4.75); somnolence 2.83 (2.05 to 3.91); loss of balance 2.62 (1.12 to 6.13); hallucination 2.19 (1.02 to 4.68); nausea 2.08 (1.63 to 2.65); asthenia 2.03 (1.35 to 3.06); fatigue 2.00 (1.54 to 2.62); vomiting 1.67 (1.13 to 2.47); diarrhoea 1.65 (1.04 to 2.62). Not significant: depression 1.32 (0.87 to 2.01), anxiety 1.98 (0.73 to 5.35), paranoia 2.05 (0.42 to 10.10), psychosis 1.09 (0.07 to 16.35), seizures 0.91 (0.05 to 15.66), dyspnoea 0.83 (0.26 to 2.63). No absolute frequencies.
